simbad-basic.name: SIMBAD Astronomical Database — CDS, Strasbourg
simbad-basic.locator: TAP/ADQL: SELECT i.id,b.main_id,b.ra,b.dec,b.plx_value,b.plx_err,b.plx_bibcode,b.sp_type,b.sp_bibcode,f.V FROM basic b JOIN ident i ON i.oidref=b.oid LEFT JOIN allfluxes f ON f.oidref=b.oid WHERE i.id IN ('* alf CMa', ...)
simbad-basic.provenance: Adopted parallaxes for all 21 objects carry bibcode 2007A&A...474..653V = van Leeuwen (2007), the Hipparcos new reduction. Exception: alf Cen A/B carry 1997A&A...323L..49P = Perryman et al. (1997).

simbad-flux.name: SIMBAD flux table — CDS, Strasbourg
simbad-flux.locator: TAP/ADQL: SELECT i.id,fl.filter,fl.flux,fl.bibcode FROM basic b JOIN ident i ON i.oidref=b.oid JOIN flux fl ON fl.oidref=b.oid WHERE fl.filter='V' AND i.id IN (...)
simbad-flux.provenance: Every V magnitude returned carries bibcode 2002yCat.2237....0D = Ducati (2002), 'Catalogue of Stellar Photometry in Johnson's 11-colour system', VizieR II/237. This is ONE photometric lineage, not a consensus.
simbad-flux.citation: Ducati 2002, VizieR On-line Data Catalog II/237

simbad-mesplx.name: SIMBAD mesPlx (all published parallaxes) — CDS, Strasbourg
simbad-mesplx.locator: TAP/ADQL: SELECT i.id,m.plx,m.plx_err,m.bibcode FROM basic b JOIN ident i ON i.oidref=b.oid JOIN mesPlx m ON m.oidref=b.oid WHERE i.id IN ('* alf Cen A','* alf Tau')

simbad-id.name: SIMBAD object query (ASCII output) — CDS, Strasbourg

hipparcos-vizier.name: Hipparcos Catalogue (ESA 1997) via VizieR I/239/hip_main — CDS
hipparcos-vizier.provenance: The ORIGINAL 1997 reduction. Superseded for parallax by I/311/hip2; retained here because several repo values trace to it. Its Vmag field is known to be poor for the very brightest stars (it gives Canopus -0.62 against -0.72/-0.74 elsewhere).

hipparcos2-vizier.name: Hipparcos, the New Reduction (van Leeuwen 2007) via VizieR I/311/hip2 — CDS

iau-csn.name: IAU Catalog of Star Names (IAU-CSN), IAU Working Group on Star Names

batches.title: Section H — the brightest stars in Earth's sky

batches.leverageRationle: Section H is the only content in the repo already policed by a machine cross-check (check-astronomy-content.mjs section [8]: profile mag vs BRIGHTNESS_RANKING within 0.02, profile distance vs NEAREST_RANKING within 0.05, magRange containment, and a hard requirement that every top-16 ranked star carry a profile). That gate compares the repo to ITSELF. It has no external anchor, so a value that is wrong in both places passes green — which is exactly what happened to alpha Centauri's distance. contradictions.where: src/starData.js#alpha-centauri-a mag: -0.01 vs BRIGHTNESS_RANKING rank 3 mag: -0.27
contradictions.problem: m1 = -0.01 and m2 = 1.33 combine to -0.2873, i.e. -0.29. The ranking says -0.27. -0.27 requires m1 = +0.01. The alpha-centauri-a entry ALSO contradicts itself: its factsAdvanced[2] says the pair 'appears to the eye as one star of magnitude -0.27' while its own mag field is -0.01.
contradictions.evidence: simbad-flux (Ducati 2002) gives A = 0.01, B = 1.33 -> -0.2714. bsc5-vizier gives A = -0.01, B = 1.33 -> -0.2873. hipparcos-vizier gives A = -0.01, B = 1.35 -> -0.2828. wikipedia-alphacen states A = '+0.01' alongside the combined '-0.27' — self-consistent; the repo copied the combined value and flipped the sign on the component.
contradictions.whyItSurvived: check-astronomy-content.mjs section [8] compares BRIGHTNESS_RANKING rows to profiles BY NAME. The row is named 'Alpha Centauri'; the profiles are 'Alpha Centauri A' and 'Alpha Centauri B'. The row is also explicitly exempted from the top-16 profile requirement. So nothing joins them and nothing checks the combination arithmetic.
contradictions.fix: Set alpha-centauri-a mag to 0.01 (Ducati 2002 / SIMBAD), keeping the ranking's -0.27 consistent. Add a gate rule: any ranking row whose note says 'Combined light of …' must reconcile against its component profiles via the flux-sum formula within 0.02.

contradictions.kind: value traceable only to an aggregator; false precision
contradictions.where: src/starData.js#alpha-centauri-a and #alpha-centauri-b distance: 4.3441, repeated in NEAREST_RANKING ranks 2 and 3
contradictions.problem: 4.3441 ly implies a parallax of 750.81 mas. SIMBAD's mesPlx table holds three published parallaxes for alpha Cen A and 750.81 is none of them: 742.12 +/- 1.4 (Perryman et al. 1997, the value SIMBAD adopts) -> 4.3948 ly; 754.81 +/- 4.11 (van Leeuwen 2007) -> 4.3211 ly; 743.0 +/- 1.3 (Pourbaix & Boffin 2016) -> 4.3896 ly. Kervella et al. 2017's widely cited 747.17 mas -> 4.3651 ly. The repo states a five-significant-figure distance that no Tier-1 determination supports, across a literature spread of 4.32-4.40 ly.
contradictions.evidence: The number IS in the Wikipedia Alpha Centauri infobox: 'Parallax 750.81 +/- 0.38 mas', 'Distance 4.344 +/- 0.002 ly'. Confirmed by direct fetch. Aggregators are not on BACKLOG's approved source list at any tier.
contradictions.whyItSurvived: NEAREST_RANKING carries the SAME 4.3441 for ranks 2 and 3, so check-astronomy-content.mjs section [8]'s profile-vs-table distance comparison passes at |0.0| < 0.05. An internal-consistency gate cannot detect a value that is wrong on both sides. This is the single clearest argument for assertion 9.5 in the README.
contradictions.fix: Adopt 4.365 ly with a cited parallax (Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, A&A 598, L7, pi = 747.17 +/- 0.61 mas) after opening that paper's body — or 4.39 ly citing Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, A&A 586, A90, which was read and states 743 mas. Either way quote to 3 significant figures, not 5, and update BOTH the profiles and NEAREST_RANKING in the same commit.

contradictions.problem: 'It rotates near 12% of breakup velocity with a ~12.5-hour period'. Vega rotates near 91% of its angular break-up rate — the figure 12% is the DEFICIT below breakup, stated as if it were the fraction. A star at 12% of breakup would not be measurably oblate, would show no gravity darkening, and could not have a 12.5-hour period; the same sentence goes on to assert 'several thousand kelvin of pole-to-equator temperature difference', which only happens at near-critical rotation. The sentence contradicts itself.
contradictions.evidence: Aufdenberg et al. 2006, ApJ 645, 664 (arXiv:astro-ph/0603327), CHARA Array + FLUOR, K' band, baselines 103-273 m: best-fitting Roche-von Zeipel gravity-darkened model has Vega at ~91% of its angular break-up rate, equatorial velocity 275 km/s, inclination 5 deg, equatorial Teff 7,900 K, pole-to-equator difference 2,250 K.
contradictions.whyItSurvived: It is prose. No structural check can see it. This is the class of error the whole schema proposal exists for.
contradictions.fix: 'It rotates at roughly 90% of its break-up velocity — about 275 km/s at the equator — on a period near 12.5 hours.' Two more sources before shipping: Peterson et al. 2006 (Nature 440, 896) and Monnier et al. 2012 (ApJ 761, L3). Also soften 'several thousand kelvin' to 'over two thousand kelvin' (Aufdenberg's 2,250 K); later CHARA/MIRC work reports less.

contradictions.evidence: Distances from hipparcos2-vizier (Canopus plx 10.55, Sirius plx 379.21); magnitude from simbad-flux (-0.74). The companion claim '36 times further away' is exactly right (35.95).
contradictions.fix: 'roughly magnitude -8.5' — which is still, correctly, bright enough to cast shadows.

contradictions.kind: table mislabelled and incomplete; two entries use incompatible definitions
contradictions.where: src/starData.js#NEAREST_RANKING (docstring: 'Nearest stellar systems by distance in light-years (ST-137)') vs #sirius factsAdvanced[0]
contradictions.problem: The table is titled 'systems' but ranks individual STARS — Alpha Centauri A and B occupy ranks 2 and 3, Sirius A and B ranks 7 and 8. It also omits the two nearest brown-dwarf systems entirely. Meanwhile the Sirius entry asserts 'at 8.6 ly it is the seventh-nearest stellar system', which is TRUE only on the system-counting convention that includes brown dwarfs — the opposite convention to the table's. The table arrives at rank 7 for Sirius A by a different and incorrect route (counting alf Cen A and B separately).
contradictions.evidence: SIMBAD sim-id: Luhman 16, parallax 501.557 +/- 0.082 mas (bibcode 2018A&A...618A.111L) -> 6.503 ly. WISE J085510.83-071442.5, parallax 439.0 +/- 2.4 mas (bibcode 2021ApJS..253....7K), object type BD*, spectral Y2 -> 7.430 ly. Both are nearer than Wolf 359 (7.856 ly) and Lalande 21185 (8.31 ly), which the table lists at ranks 5 and 6.
contradictions.fix: Pick one convention and state it in the docstring. If 'systems': merge alf Cen A/B and Sirius A/B into single rows, insert Luhman 16 (6.50 ly) and WISE 0855-0714 (7.43 ly), and Sirius becomes rank 5 of the resulting star-only list or rank 7 with brown dwarfs included — say which. If 'stars': rename the export and the docstring, and fix the Sirius fact instead. NOTE: this is Section G, outside batch STB-H-001's scope; reported because it was found while verifying a Section H claim.

contradictions.kind: contested value presented as settled; unsourced superlative
contradictions.problem: 'its equatorial radius exceeds its polar radius by more than 50% — the most oblate star measured' / 'It is the least round star we know of.' The 1.56 ratio is real and published, but it exceeds 1.5 — the maximum a rigidly rotating Roche model allows — which is why the result was immediately argued over rather than accepted. Carciofi et al. 2008 fit the same data with a critically rotating star plus a small equatorial disk, moving part of the apparent excess off the photosphere.
contradictions.evidence: Domiciano de Souza et al. 2003, A&A 407, L47 (arXiv:astro-ph/0306277): 2a/2b = 1.56 +/- 0.05 from VLTI-VINCI. Carciofi et al. 2008, ApJ 676, L41 (arXiv:0801.4901): critically rotating star + equatorial disk. Kervella et al. 2022, A&A 667, A111: Achernar A is in 'a short-lived phase … during which its geometrical flattening ratio is the most extreme' — supporting extreme flattening without endorsing 1.56.
contradictions.fix: Attribute rather than assert: 'VLTI interferometry in 2003 measured an equatorial-to-polar ratio of 1.56, above what a rigidly rotating model allows; later work attributes part of that to a thin equatorial disk.' Drop or source the superlative — Regulus and several Be stars are also near-critical rotators.

contradictions.problem: Three published parallaxes give 66.64, 65.11 and 65.23 ly — a 2.3% spread. 65.3 is traceable (Gatewood 2008 gives 65.23; the 1997 Hipparcos reduction gives 65.11) but disagrees with the value SIMBAD adopts and serves. The number is stated flat, to three significant figures, with no uncertainty and no note.
contradictions.evidence: simbad-mesplx for alf Tau: 48.94 +/- 0.77 mas (2007A&A...474..653V) -> 66.644 ly; 50.09 +/- 0.95 (1997A&A...323L..49P) -> 65.114 ly; 50.0 +/- 1.3 (2008AJ....136..452G, Gatewood 2008) -> 65.231 ly. Contrast Achernar in the same section, where the repo correctly uses the 2007 reduction over the 1997 one.
contradictions.fix: Either 66.6 ly citing van Leeuwen 2007, or keep 65.3 and say why (Gatewood's ground-based astrometry) — but not a bare number. The dependent claim 'less than half the Hyades' distance' holds either way.

contradictions.kind: the module's own uncertainty convention applied inconsistently
contradictions.problem: starData.js's header says supergiant distances 'remain genuinely uncertain and say so rather than quoting false precision', and the module carries a distanceUncertain flag for exactly this. Betelgeuse (parallax error 12.7%) and Deneb (13.9%) and Mu Cephei and UY Scuti all carry it. Antares' parallax error is 17.0% — the largest of any profiled star that does NOT carry the flag. Rigel's is 9.0%, also unflagged.
contradictions.evidence: hipparcos2-vizier: Antares 5.89 +/- 1.00 mas (spans ~474-667 ly); Betelgeuse 6.55 +/- 0.83; Rigel 3.78 +/- 0.34; Deneb 2.31 +/- 0.32.
contradictions.fix: Add distanceUncertain: true to antares and rigel, or define the threshold explicitly and let a gate apply it: flag when e_Plx/Plx > 0.10.

contradictions.kind: the Antares bug, structurally unfixed on a different star
contradictions.problem: The entry's own factsAdvanced[0] calls Spica 'a rotating ellipsoidal variable' whose 'changing projected area produces the light variation'. It then states mag: 0.97 with NO magRange. Section [8]'s magRange-containment check therefore has nothing to check, and 0.97 is the bright end: BSC5, Hipparcos and IAU-CSN all give 0.98. This is precisely the failure that produced the Antares mag 0.6 defect — a variable star assigned its bright extreme as a flat magnitude — reproduced on a star where the fix was never applied.
contradictions.fix: Set mag: 0.98 and add magRange (Spica's ellipsoidal variation is roughly 0.97-1.04; source it before writing the numbers). Generalise the gate: any entry whose facts contain 'variable' should be required to carry magRange.

contradictions.kind: unremarked tie in a ranking that claims to be ordered
contradictions.problem: Both are exactly 1.25 in all four sources checked. The table orders them 19 and 20 with no tiebreak note, while it does annotate every other awkward case ('Variable; rank shifts…', 'Combined light of…').
contradictions.evidence: simbad-basic, bsc5-vizier, hipparcos-vizier and iau-csn all give 1.25 for both alf Cyg and bet Cru.
contradictions.fix: Add a note to one of them, or carry mags to three decimals. Gate rule 9.10 in the README would catch this class automatically.

antares 'placed at the Sun its surface would reach past the orbit of Mars' — 680 R☉ = 3.16 AU vs Mars at 1.52 AU. Implication verified; the 680 R☉ input is not yet sourced.
